stem: Which set of functional groups would you expect to find on a fully hydrophilic region of a biological molecule?
options: Hydroxyl and phosphate
Methyl and methyl
Methyl and hydroxyl
Methyl and carbonyl (nonpolar context)
None of the above — all functional groups are equally hydrophobic
explanation: Hydroxyl and phosphate groups are both polar/charged and interact favorably with water, making them hydrophilic; methyl is nonpolar/hydrophobic and wouldn't belong in a "fully hydrophilic" set.

stem: Which of the following correctly completes this statement: "A condensation reaction ___, while a hydrolysis reaction ___."
options: consumes water and releases energy / releases water and requires energy input
requires no water at all / also requires no water
releases energy without involving water / consumes energy without involving water
releases water and requires energy input / consumes water and releases energy
only occurs in carbohydrates / only occurs in proteins
explanation: Condensation joins monomers by releasing a water molecule and requires energy input; hydrolysis is the reverse — it consumes water and releases energy as it breaks a bond.

stem: A mutation changes one amino acid's R group from a nonpolar, hydrophobic one to a charged, hydrophilic one, in a region normally buried in the protein's hydrophobic core. What is the most likely consequence?
options: No effect, since all amino acids are interchangeable
The protein's overall amino acid count changes
The protein automatically gains a new enzymatic function
The primary structure becomes undefined
The protein may misfold, since a charged R group is unstable in a hydrophobic core environment
explanation: R-group chemistry drives folding — placing a charged, hydrophilic group into a hydrophobic core disrupts the interactions stabilizing that fold, making misfolding the most likely consequence; amino acid identity/count are unrelated to this change, and new function or "undefined" sequence aren't real consequences of a single substitution.

stem: Which of the following correctly lists all three structural components of a single nucleotide?
options: A nitrogenous base, an amino acid, and a phosphate group
A nitrogenous base, a five-carbon sugar, and a phosphate group
A five-carbon sugar, a fatty acid tail, and a phosphate group
A nitrogenous base, a five-carbon sugar, and a glycosidic bond
Two nitrogenous bases and one sugar
explanation: A nucleotide is defined by exactly these three parts — base, sugar, phosphate; the other options substitute in components (amino acid, fatty acid tail) or relationships (glycosidic bond, a second base) that don't belong in this structural definition.
links: The three parts of a nucleotide

stem: Glucose and fructose are combined to form sucrose. Which term correctly describes the resulting molecule, and which reaction type formed it?
options: Polysaccharide, formed by hydrolysis
Monosaccharide, formed by condensation
Disaccharide, formed by condensation
Disaccharide, formed by hydrolysis
Oligosaccharide, formed by hydrolysis
explanation: Two monosaccharides joined together form a disaccharide, and joining monomers together (releasing water) is a condensation reaction.

stem: Which of the following best explains why lipids, unlike carbohydrates, proteins, and nucleic acids, are not classified as polymers?
options: Lipids are not built from a single repeating monomer joined by a consistent bond type
Lipids don't contain carbon
Lipids are too large to be polymers
Lipids don't participate in condensation or hydrolysis reactions at all
Lipids only exist inside membranes
explanation: The other three macromolecule classes are polymers of a repeating monomer (amino acids, nucleotides, monosaccharides); lipids are grouped by a shared property (hydrophobicity) rather than being built from one consistent repeating monomer, so they don't fit the polymer definition.

stem: Which of the following correctly describes why carbon, rather than another element, forms the structural backbone of nearly all biological macromolecules?
options: Carbon is the most abundant element in the universe
Carbon cannot form double bonds, which makes its structures more stable
Carbon only bonds with oxygen
Carbon's four valence electrons let it form up to four stable covalent bonds, enabling chains, rings, and branches
Carbon has no valence electrons, so it doesn't need to bond at all
explanation: Carbon's four valence electrons give it up to four bonding sites, enabling the vast structural diversity (chains, rings, branches) that underlies biological macromolecules — none of the other statements are accurate.
links: Why carbon is the backbone element

stem: Which of the following pairs would most likely form an ionic bond rather than a covalent bond?
options: Two carbon atoms
A carbon atom and a hydrogen atom
Two oxygen atoms
A carbon atom and an oxygen atom
A sodium atom and a chlorine atom
explanation: Ionic bonds form between atoms with a very large electronegativity difference, where electrons transfer rather than share — sodium (very low electronegativity) and chlorine (very high) is the classic case; the other pairs share electrons covalently.

stem: A solution's pH drops from 8 to 5. What has happened to the H+ ion concentration?
options: It decreased 3-fold
It increased 1,000-fold
It decreased 1,000-fold
It increased 3-fold
It stayed the same, since pH only measures OH- concentration
explanation: pH is a negative log scale; dropping 3 units (8→5) means H+ concentration increased by 10³ = 1,000-fold.

stem: A researcher studying E. coli wants to directly observe the coupling between transcription and translation — both processes happening on the same mRNA, at the same time, in the same compartment. Which feature of E. coli's cell biology makes this observable?
options: Its cell wall is made of peptidoglycan
It reproduces by binary fission
It lacks a nuclear envelope separating DNA from ribosomes
It has plasmids in addition to its main chromosome
It thrives in extreme environments
explanation: Without a nuclear envelope, E. coli's DNA and ribosomes share the same compartment, allowing transcription and translation to occur simultaneously on the same mRNA — a hallmark of prokaryotic gene expression not possible in a eukaryotic cell with a nucleus.

stem: Mitochondria and chloroplasts both have a double membrane, yet both are classified as non-EMS organelles. Which principle best explains why?
options: EMS classification depends specifically on participation in the ER–Golgi–vesicle trafficking pathway, not on possessing a membrane
EMS classification depends on the number of membranes an organelle has
Mitochondria and chloroplasts don't actually have any membrane at all
Only organelles found in plant cells can be EMS
EMS status depends on whether the organelle contains DNA
explanation: The EMS criterion is trafficking-pathway participation, not membrane count — mitochondria and chloroplasts have membranes (two each, in fact) but no connection to the ER–Golgi–vesicle network, and their membranes instead reflect endosymbiotic bacterial origin.

stem: Which of the following correctly describes both the basic structure of an atom and how a covalent bond forms between two atoms?
options: An atom has protons and electrons only (no neutrons); a covalent bond forms when one atom fully donates an electron to another
An atom has a nucleus of electrons surrounded by protons and neutrons; a covalent bond forms when atoms repel each other's electrons
An atom has a nucleus of protons and neutrons surrounded by electrons; a covalent bond forms when two atoms share a pair of valence electrons
An atom has no internal structure; a covalent bond forms only between identical atoms
An atom's mass comes entirely from its electrons; a covalent bond forms by transferring neutrons
explanation: An atom's nucleus (protons + neutrons) is surrounded by electrons in shells/orbitals; a covalent bond specifically forms when two atoms share a pair of valence electrons, as opposed to the full transfer that defines an ionic bond.

stem: A scientist wants to track the location of a specific protein inside living cells over time, distinguishing it from every other protein in the cell. Which imaging approach is best suited to this, and why?
options: Standard light microscopy, because it requires no special preparation
Electron microscopy, because it has the highest possible resolution
X-ray crystallography, because it reveals atomic-level detail
None of these — individual proteins cannot be visualized by any microscopy technique
Fluorescence microscopy, because a fluorescent tag can selectively label just that one protein against a dark background
explanation: Fluorescence microscopy's key advantage is selective labeling — tagging one specific molecule so it lights up while everything else stays dark — exactly what's needed to track one protein among many; the other techniques either lack this specificity or aren't suited to live, protein-level tracking.

stem: ATP is built from adenine, ribose, and three phosphate groups. Which part of this structure is specifically where the "high energy" of ATP is stored?
options: The bonds between the second and third phosphate groups
The bond between adenine and ribose
The ribose sugar ring itself
The bond between the first phosphate and ribose
ATP does not actually store any usable energy
explanation: ATP's structure is adenine + ribose + three phosphates, and the high-energy bonds specifically linking the 2nd and 3rd phosphates are what release usable energy when hydrolyzed (ATP→ADP).

stem: Which of the following best describes the cytoskeleton's primary role in a eukaryotic cell?
options: It synthesizes proteins from mRNA
It stores the cell's genetic material
It generates ATP through cellular respiration
It provides structural support and enables mechanical activities like transport and movement
It packages proteins for secretion
explanation: The cytoskeleton is a protein filament network that provides structural support and drives mechanical activities (transport, movement, division) — not protein synthesis, genetic storage, ATP generation, or secretion packaging, which are other structures' jobs.

stem: The amide functional group is specifically responsible for which biologically important linkage?
options: The glycosidic bond between two monosaccharides
The peptide bond between two amino acids
The phosphodiester bond between two nucleotides
The disulfide bond between two cysteines
The ester bond between glycerol and a fatty acid
explanation: The amide functional group is exactly what forms the peptide bond linking amino acids together into a polypeptide chain.

stem: In aqueous solution, glucose predominantly exists not as an open chain but as a ring. Which bond formation is responsible for this cyclization?
options: A glycosidic bond between two separate glucose molecules
A peptide bond within the glucose molecule
A disulfide bond between two carbons in the chain
A phosphodiester bond linking C1 to a phosphate group
A bond forming between glucose's C1 and C5 (via its oxygen), closing the chain into a ring
explanation: Cyclic monosaccharide formation happens when the aldehyde carbon (C1) reacts intramolecularly with the hydroxyl on C5, closing the chain into a ring — a different, intramolecular event from the (intermolecular) glycosidic bond that later links separate sugars.

stem: A polypeptide chain and a strand of RNA are both broken down into their monomers. Which statement correctly describes what these two breakdown reactions have in common?
options: Both are hydrolysis reactions that consume water, reversing the same type of condensation reaction that built each polymer
Neither reaction involves water
Both are condensation reactions that release water
Only the polypeptide breakdown involves water; RNA breakdown does not
Both reactions require the addition of a phosphate group
explanation: Both proteins and nucleic acids are polymers built by condensation (releasing water) and broken down by hydrolysis (consuming water) — the same reversible condensation/hydrolysis logic applies across all macromolecule classes, not just one.

stem: Property 1 (membrane-enclosed cytoplasm) and an enzyme's ability to fold correctly both depend on a chemistry principle that spans Modules 1 and 2. Which principle is it?
options: The number of chromosomes in the cell's nucleus
The rate of ATP production during glycolysis
How specific functional groups interact with water — polarity and charge — which governs both phospholipid self-assembly into a membrane and R-group interactions that stabilize protein folding
Whether the organism is unicellular or multicellular
The presence or absence of a cell wall
explanation: Both phenomena trace back to functional-group chemistry — polarity and charge relative to water. Phospholipids self-assemble into a membrane because they're amphipathic (polar head, nonpolar tails), and a protein's fold is stabilized by charge/polarity interactions between R groups, which pH can disrupt.

stem: Which of the following pairs correctly links a Module 1 concept to the specific mechanism or classification that explains it?
options: Tenet 3 ↔ explained by the cytoskeleton's membrane structure
Tenet 3 (cells from pre-existing cells) ↔ explained at the prokaryotic level by binary fission, which duplicates DNA before dividing
The cytoskeleton's mechanical role ↔ explained by its classification as EMS
Binary fission ↔ explained by the cytoskeleton organizing vesicle trafficking
The cytoskeleton's non-EMS classification ↔ explained by its role in DNA replication
explanation: Binary fission — DNA duplication followed by division into two cells — is the prokaryotic-level instance of tenet 3. The cytoskeleton, by contrast, has no membrane and is classified non-EMS despite its essential mechanical/support role; the other pairings mismatch cause and explanation.

stem: Which statement correctly connects a basic cell property (from Module 1) to a Module 2 chemistry concept?
options: Property 1 (membrane) is explained by all four macromolecule classes being organic — i.e., carbon-containing
Property 2 (genetic program) has nothing to do with nucleotide-level chemistry, since it operates only at the whole-cell level
The central dogma explains property 6 (mechanical activity), not property 2
All four macromolecule classes (carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, nucleic acids) are organic because each contains carbon, which is why "organic molecule" simply means "contains carbon"
Carbon content is irrelevant to whether a molecule counts as a macromolecule
explanation: All four macromolecule classes qualify as organic specifically because each contains carbon — the literal definition of "organic" used here. Property 2 (the genetic program), in turn, is implemented through the central dogma at the nucleotide level — DNA→RNA→protein — connecting the cell-level property directly to Module 2's chemistry.

stem: A course covers seven model organisms, each chosen to make a specific biological process easier to study. Which reasoning correctly matches a model organism to what it's used for?
options: Mus musculus is used mainly to study rapid genetic screening because of its short generation time
E. coli is used to study the eukaryotic cell cycle because it has the simplest genome
S. cerevisiae is used to study a minimal, tractable model of the eukaryotic cell cycle
C. elegans is used mainly to study mammalian-specific development
Arabidopsis is used to study prokaryotic gene expression
explanation: Each model organism is chosen for a specific fit: yeast (S. cerevisiae) as a minimal eukaryote for cell-cycle study; mouse for rapid genetic screening/mammalian translation; E. coli for prokaryotic DNA/RNA/protein processes; C. elegans for cell lineage tracking; Arabidopsis for flowering-plant biology — matching organism to purpose, not interchangeably.

stem: Which of the following correctly describes where an atom's protons and neutrons are located relative to its electrons?
options: Protons and neutrons orbit around a central cloud of electrons
Protons, neutrons, and electrons are all located in the nucleus
Protons and neutrons make up the nucleus, while electrons occupy the surrounding space in shells
Only electrons exist in an atom; protons and neutrons are found in molecules, not atoms
Protons are in the nucleus, but neutrons and electrons both orbit outside it
explanation: The nucleus (protons + neutrons) sits at the atom's center, while electrons occupy the surrounding space in shells/orbitals — the standard atomic structure.
links: Atomic structure: nucleus vs electron shells

stem: Two hydrogen atoms come together to form H2. Which statement correctly describes the resulting bond?
options: Each hydrogen atom fully transfers its electron to the other
No bond forms, since hydrogen has no valence electrons to share
The two atoms share a pair of valence electrons between them, forming a covalent bond
The atoms form an ionic bond due to their different electronegativities
The bond forms from proton-to-proton attraction alone
explanation: A covalent bond is defined by two atoms sharing a pair of valence electrons — exactly what happens as two hydrogen atoms each contribute one electron to a shared pair in H2.

stem: The diagram shows three circular fields of view side by side. The fluorescence panel is almost entirely black except for one small glowing spot near the center. A student argues this means fluorescence microscopy has worse resolution than electron microscopy, since "you can barely see anything." What is wrong with that reasoning?
options: Fluorescence microscopy really does have worse resolution than EM, so the student is correct
The dark field isn't a resolution limit — it's the point: only the tagged structure emits light, so everything else is invisible by design
EM images are always false-color, so the two panels can't be fairly compared
Fluorescence microscopy can only be performed on tissue that has already been sectioned by EM, so the comparison is circular
The three panels must be at different magnifications, which is the actual reason less is visible
explanation: Fluorescence microscopy's "mostly dark" appearance comes from selective labeling — only molecules bound to the fluorescent tag glow, so an unlabeled structure stays invisible even though it's physically there. That's a deliberate trade for specificity, not a resolution failure. EM's fine ultrastructure detail comes from a different trade-off entirely: a much shorter effective wavelength, but only on a fixed (dead) sample.
links: Fluorescence microscopy · Light microscopy · Electron microscopy

box: In the diagram, an arrow traces a path from the rough ER through the Golgi to a vesicle budding toward the plasma membrane. The mitochondrion and chloroplast are drawn off to the side, each with a visibly doubled outline, next to the note "double membrane, but no vesicle traffic with the EMS."
claim: Mitochondria and chloroplasts are excluded from the EMS specifically because their membranes are structurally too different (double vs. single) to physically fuse with EMS vesicles.
explanation: The diagram's note names the real criterion: whether a compartment participates in the traced vesicle-trafficking pathway — not how many membranes it has. Mitochondria and chloroplasts are excluded because they're topologically disconnected from that pathway (most of their proteins are made on free ribosomes and imported directly), not because a double membrane is somehow incompatible with vesicle fusion.

title: Reading the two cell diagrams side by side
stem: Study the Prokaryote and Eukaryote diagrams below. Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) The prokaryote diagram shows small circles labeled "plasmids" near the nucleoid, plus a thick outer boundary labeled "cell wall + plasma membrane."

(나) The eukaryote diagram shows a labeled "nucleus" region and several thin unlabeled lines in the cytoplasm.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: The plasmids shown in the prokaryote diagram are separate from the cell's main chromosome and are not required for the cell's basic survival.
statements.explanation: Plasmids carry supplementary genes (e.g., antibiotic resistance) — useful under certain conditions but not essential to core survival, unlike the main circular chromosome.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: The thin lines drawn in the eukaryote diagram most likely represent cytoskeletal filaments, a structural feature the prokaryote diagram doesn't include.
statements.explanation: Prokaryotes lack a true cytoskeleton and rely on the cell wall for structural support instead; the eukaryote diagram's internal lines represent the cytoskeleton that eukaryotic cells use.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Because the eukaryote diagram shows a membrane-enclosed nucleus, the diagram indicates eukaryotic cells are evolutionarily superior to prokaryotic cells.
statements.explanation: A nuclear envelope is a structural difference in compartmentalization, not a claim about evolutionary "superiority" — prokaryotes are not an incomplete version of eukaryotes; they're an independently successful domain-level lineage.

links: Prokaryote vs eukaryote · Plasmids · Cytoskeleton · Cell wall

box: In the diagram, the branch point for Eukarya sits ON the Archaea branch, partway between the Bacteria/Archaea split and the Archaea tip — not on its own separate branch straight from the root.
claim: This branching pattern shown in the diagram means Eukarya and Bacteria are the two domains most distantly related to each other.
explanation: Since Eukarya branches from within Archaea (a genuinely surprising, well-supported modern finding), Eukarya and Archaea share a more recent common ancestor than either does with Bacteria — making Bacteria the domain most distantly related to both. This contradicts a naive "three equally-spaced branches" reading, which is exactly why the diagram draws the branch point where it does rather than as three separate lines from one root.
links: Three-domain tree · Eukarya from within Archaea

stem: In the diagram, the plant cell is drawn as a rigid square with arrows pushing outward from the central vacuole against the outer wall, while the animal cell is drawn as an irregular rounded shape with no such outward arrows. What does this visual contrast best illustrate?
options: Plant cells are simply larger than animal cells
Only plant cells contain a nucleus

The plant cell's rigid shape comes from turgor pressure (the vacuole pushing outward against the wall), while the animal cell's rounded, flexible shape is held by its cytoskeleton instead, with no wall to push against
Animal cells cannot survive in water, unlike plant cells
The vacuole shown in the plant cell is an EMS structure absent from all animal cells
explanation: The outward arrows in the plant-cell diagram represent turgor pressure — water entering the central vacuole pushes the plasma membrane against the rigid cell wall, keeping the cell firm. Animal cells have neither a wall nor a large central vacuole, so they can't develop turgor pressure; their shape is instead maintained by the cytoskeleton, which is why the diagram draws them as flexible and rounded rather than boxy.
links: Plant cell turgor pressure · Animal cell shape · Cytoskeleton

title: Placing real bonds on the spectrum
stem: The diagram places three example bonds — C–H, O–H (water), and Na–Cl — at different points along one continuous spectrum from "nonpolar covalent" to "ionic." Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) C–H sits at the far left of the spectrum, in the nonpolar covalent zone.

(나) Na–Cl sits at the far right, in the ionic zone.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Placing these three bonds on ONE continuous spectrum, rather than in three separate unconnected boxes, reflects that polarity and ionic character differ in degree (ΔEN), not in kind.
statements.explanation: Bond character is a continuum based on the electronegativity difference between the two atoms — there's no sharp cutoff, just increasing charge separation as ΔEN grows, which is why one continuous spectrum is the accurate way to draw it.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: O–H in water sits in the middle "polar covalent" zone because oxygen and hydrogen still share their bonding electrons, just unequally, unlike Na–Cl where an electron is essentially fully transferred.
statements.explanation: Polar covalent bonds are still bonds of shared electrons — just with unequal sharing due to a real but moderate ΔEN. Ionic bonds involve a large enough ΔEN that an electron is essentially transferred rather than shared.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Since C–H and Na–Cl fall at opposite ends of the same spectrum, C–H must also be capable of dissolving in water via hydration shells, the same way NaCl does.
statements.explanation: Hydration shells form around charged/highly polar species because water's partial charges can orient toward them; C–H's near-zero ΔEN means the bond carries no meaningful partial charge for water to interact with electrostatically, so nonpolar C–H-rich molecules do NOT dissolve this way.

links: Electronegativity spectrum · Polar vs nonpolar covalent · Hydration shells

box: The diagram draws solid lines for the two O–H bonds inside a single water molecule, and dashed lines connecting that molecule's H atoms to O atoms on two neighboring (partial) molecules.
claim: If you boiled away all of a water sample's hydrogen bonds while leaving every covalent O–H bond intact, you would be left with intact water molecules that are simply no longer clustered together — not a pile of separated hydrogen and oxygen atoms.
explanation: This is exactly the solid-vs-dashed distinction the diagram encodes: the solid covalent O–H bonds (strong, inside one molecule) are what make something "a water molecule" at all, while the dashed hydrogen bonds (weak, between molecules) are what hold separate water molecules to each other. Boiling breaks hydrogen bonds, not covalent bonds — steam is still made of intact H2O molecules, just no longer hydrogen-bonded into a liquid network.
links: Hydrogen bonds vs covalent bonds · Water polarity

stem: In the diagram, the water molecules surrounding Na+ all point their oxygen (δ–) end inward, while the water molecules surrounding Cl– all point a hydrogen (δ+) end inward. Why does the diagram orient them this way, rather than randomly?
options: Water molecules always orient the same way regardless of what they're surrounding
Opposite charges attract: an ion's charge orients the nearest partial charge on each water molecule toward it, so oxygen's δ– faces the cation and hydrogen's δ+ faces the anion
The orientation shown is arbitrary and has no chemical basis
Na+ and Cl– are both attracted to the same end of the water molecule
This orientation only occurs at very low temperatures
explanation: Water's polarity (oxygen slightly negative, hydrogens slightly positive) means each water molecule acts like a tiny magnet. Electrostatic attraction dictates the orientation: the electron-rich oxygen end is drawn toward the positively charged Na+, while a hydrogen end is drawn toward the negatively charged Cl–. This ordered shell of oriented water molecules is exactly what "dissolving" an ionic compound means at the molecular level.
links: Hydration shells · Water dissolves NaCl · Ion–dipole attraction

box: The diagram shows methane's four C–H pulls as arrows pointing symmetrically outward in four directions from a central carbon, versus water's two O–H pulls both pointing away from oxygen on the same side, summing into one net downward arrow.
claim: If methane's four C–H bonds were rearranged to point in only two directions instead of four (like water's bent shape), methane would become a polar molecule even though each individual C–H bond stayed exactly as nonpolar as before.
explanation: This is the diagram's central point: whether a molecule is polar depends on molecular geometry (how individual bond dipoles are arranged in space), not only on how polar each individual bond is. Water's bent shape lets its two O–H dipoles sum rather than cancel; methane's symmetric shape lets its four C–H dipoles cancel exactly. Change the geometry to something asymmetric and even weakly polar bonds would stop canceling, producing a net dipole.
links: Molecular geometry and polarity · Methane symmetric cancellation · Water net dipole

title: Reading the pH scale quantitatively
stem: The diagram places gastric acid (~pH 2), coffee (~pH 5), blood (~pH 7.4), baking soda (~pH 9), and bleach (~pH 13) along a 0–14 scale, with a note that each whole step is a 10× change in [H+]. Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Gastric acid sits at ~pH 2.

(나) Coffee sits at ~pH 5, three whole steps higher on the scale.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Based on the diagram's own note, gastric acid's H+ concentration is approximately 1,000 times higher than coffee's.
statements.explanation: 3 pH units apart = 10³ = 1,000× difference in [H+], exactly as the diagram's caption states.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Blood's position on the diagram, just above the exact center of the 0–14 scale, means blood is on the basic side of neutral, the same general direction as baking soda.
statements.explanation: pH 7.4 is slightly above neutral (7), placing blood on the basic side of neutral, same general direction as baking soda (~9), even though blood's H+ concentration is far closer to neutral than baking soda's.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Because bleach is drawn near the opposite end of the scale from gastric acid, bleach and gastric acid must have roughly the same magnitude of [H+] difference from pure water (pH 7).
statements.explanation: Gastric acid (pH 2) is 5 units from neutral; bleach (pH 13) is 6 units from neutral — close but not equal, and since the scale is logarithmic that's a 10-fold difference in how far each one's [H+] actually sits from water's.

links: pH scale · Logarithmic H+ concentration · Real-world pH reference points

stem: In the diagram's right-hand panel, one amino acid's –COOH group and a second amino acid's H2N– group are joined by an arrow labeled "peptide bond," with "+ H2O released" written below. Which of the following correctly identifies what happened to the atoms at the reaction site?
options: The –COOH group's –OH and one H from the –NH2 group left together as part of the released water molecule, and the remaining carbon and nitrogen are now directly bonded
An entire water molecule was inserted between the two amino acids to link them
The peptide bond forms by transferring an electron from nitrogen to carbon, making it an ionic bond
Both R groups were consumed in the reaction, which is why they aren't shown in this panel
The reaction shown is hydrolysis, not condensation, since a small molecule (water) is a product
explanation: Peptide bond formation is a condensation (dehydration synthesis) reaction: the –OH from the carboxyl group and one H from the amino group are removed and combine to form the released H2O, while the remaining carbonyl carbon and amine nitrogen form the new C–N peptide bond. (Option E correctly names water as a product but wrongly calls the reaction hydrolysis — hydrolysis consumes water to break a bond; this reaction releases water to form one, which is condensation.)
links: Peptide bond formation · Condensation reaction · Zwitterion

box: The diagram draws four panels in sequence: a beaded chain (Primary), a coiled ribbon (Secondary), a single folded blob (Tertiary), and two differently-shaded blobs touching each other (Quaternary).
claim: Based on how the diagram progresses, a protein must pass through all four levels in order, and a single-chain protein that never forms multi-subunit assemblies is therefore an "incomplete" or defective protein.
explanation: The four levels describe increasing layers of structural organization that build on each other conceptually (sequence → local folding → overall 3D shape → assembly with other chains), but quaternary structure only applies to proteins made of multiple polypeptide chains. A fully functional single-chain protein (like myoglobin) simply has no quaternary level to reach — it is not defective or incomplete for stopping at tertiary structure.
links: Levels of protein structure · Quaternary structure requires multiple chains

title: Ring structure and nucleotide anatomy together
stem: The diagram shows one nucleotide's three parts (phosphate–sugar–base) alongside a separate comparison of purine (double-ring) vs. pyrimidine (single-ring) bases. Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) The nucleotide panel shows the base attached to the sugar, with the phosphate attached to the sugar on the opposite side.

(나) The purine panel shows two fused rings; the pyrimidine panel shows one ring.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Removing only the base shown in the nucleotide panel, while keeping the phosphate and sugar attached to each other, would leave a molecule that is neither a nucleoside nor a nucleotide in the standard sense.
statements.explanation: A nucleotide is specifically base + sugar + phosphate together; a nucleoside is base + sugar (no phosphate). Sugar + phosphate with no base isn't standard nucleotide terminology — the base is required for either term to apply.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: If the base drawn in the nucleotide panel were adenine, the diagram's purine panel (double ring) would be the correct structural category for it, not the pyrimidine panel.
statements.explanation: Adenine and guanine are purines (double-ring); cytosine, thymine, and uracil are pyrimidines (single-ring) — adenine belongs in the double-ring category the diagram draws.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Because both purines and pyrimidines are drawn as rings in the diagram, both categories contain the same number of nitrogen atoms per ring.
statements.explanation: The diagram deliberately draws purines with two fused rings and pyrimidines with one specifically because they differ in ring structure — this is a structural classification, and it does not imply identical atom counts between the two categories.

links: Nucleotide anatomy · Purines vs pyrimidines · Nucleoside vs nucleotide

stem: The diagram shows a backbone of alternating phosphate and sugar units, labeled 5' at the left end and 3' at the right end, with an arrow below reading "synthesis always proceeds 5'→3'." If a new nucleotide is added to extend this strand, at which end does the diagram indicate it must be added, and why?
options: At the 5' end, because that's where the existing phosphates are
At the 3' end, because each new nucleotide's phosphate bonds to the free 3'-OH already at that end of the growing chain
At either end equally, since the diagram shows the backbone as symmetric
In the middle of the strand, since that's the most chemically accessible position
At the 3' end, because that end lacks a phosphate group entirely
explanation: The diagram's labeled 5'→3' arrow reflects the chemistry of the phosphodiester bond itself: each new nucleotide's 5'-phosphate bonds to the free 3'-OH at the growing strand's end. That consumes the free 3'-OH and creates a new one on the just-added nucleotide's sugar, so growth can only continue at that end — which is why synthesis direction is always described as 5'→3', never the reverse.
links: Phosphodiester bonds · Strand directionality · 5' to 3' synthesis

box: The diagram's left panel shows a dashed curved line connecting C1 to the C5-OH of the same linear sugar, closing it into a ring. The right panel shows two rings connected by a single bond labeled "glycosidic bond," with "condensation → +H2O released" written below.
claim: The ring-closing step in the left panel and the ring-joining step in the right panel are the same type of reaction — condensation — just occurring within one molecule instead of between two.
explanation: Both are condensation reactions: intramolecular ring closure (C1's carbonyl reacting with C5's hydroxyl within the same glucose molecule) and intermolecular glycosidic bond formation (C1 of one ringed sugar reacting with an –OH of a second sugar) both form a new C–O bond while releasing a water molecule. The diagram's right-panel caption describes a reaction that is mechanistically the same category as the ring closure shown on the left, just between two separate monosaccharides instead of within one.
links: Cyclic monosaccharide formation · Glycosidic bond · Condensation reaction

title: Three lipids, one diagram
stem: The diagram places triacylglycerol, phospholipid, and cholesterol side by side, then adds a bottom panel contrasting a straight saturated tail with a kinked unsaturated tail. Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) The phospholipid icon is the only one of the three drawn with a distinct "head" shape separate from its tails.

(나) The bottom panel shows the unsaturated tail bending sharply at one point, unlike the saturated tail's straight line.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: The distinct head shown only on the phospholipid icon represents the phosphate-containing group, which is what makes phospholipids amphipathic while triacylglycerol (all tails, no head) is not.
statements.explanation: Triacylglycerol is 3 fatty acid tails on a glycerol backbone — uniformly hydrophobic, no polar head. Phospholipids swap one fatty acid for a phosphate-containing head group, creating a molecule with both a hydrophilic head and hydrophobic tails: amphipathic.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: The kink drawn in the unsaturated tail is caused by a double bond, which prevents free rotation at that point in the carbon chain.
statements.explanation: A C=C double bond is rigid and doesn't rotate the way a single bond does, which forces a fixed bend in the chain at that point — exactly the kink the diagram draws.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Because cholesterol is drawn with fused rings instead of a glycerol-and-tails structure like the other two, cholesterol is not classified as a lipid in this diagram's scheme.
statements.explanation: Lipids are grouped by a shared property — hydrophobicity — not by shared structure, which is exactly why cholesterol (rings), triacylglycerol (glycerol + 3 tails), and phospholipid (glycerol + 2 tails + head) can all sit in the same "lipid family" comparison despite having no structural blueprint in common.

links: Lipid family comparison · Amphipathic phospholipids · Saturated vs unsaturated · Lipids grouped by hydrophobicity

box: The diagram shows two rows of head circles (top and bottom), each row's tails pointing inward toward a shared middle region labeled "hydrophobic tails hidden inside," with "water (outside)" above and "water (cytoplasm)" below.
claim: This arrangement is the direct, predictable consequence of phospholipids being amphipathic and placed in a watery environment on both sides — no additional cellular machinery is required to assemble this basic structure.
explanation: This is spontaneous self-assembly: amphipathic phospholipids placed in water will spontaneously orient their hydrophilic heads toward the water on each side and cluster their hydrophobic tails away from water in the middle, because that arrangement minimizes unfavorable contact between the tails and water. The diagram's two-row, tails-inward structure is exactly the energetically favorable outcome amphipathic molecules fall into on their own — cells don't need to actively build this geometry piece by piece.
links: Amphipathic self-assembly · Phospholipid bilayer · Membrane needs amphipathic phospholipids

stem: The diagram labels the arrow from Gene (DNA) to RNA as "transcription / phosphodiester bonds" and the arrow from RNA to Protein as "translation / peptide bonds," with a note that both steps are condensation reactions. What single underlying chemical fact does this diagram use to connect two otherwise separate topics — nucleic acid chemistry and protein chemistry — into one story?
options: DNA and protein are made of the same monomers
Both transcription and translation happen in the same cellular location

Both steps build a polymer by the same general reaction type — condensation, forming a new covalent bond and releasing water — even though the specific bond formed (phosphodiester vs. peptide) and the monomer involved (nucleotide vs. amino acid) are completely different
Both arrows in the diagram represent hydrolysis reactions
RNA and protein have identical monomer-to-monomer bond geometry
explanation: The diagram's real point isn't that nucleic acids and proteins are chemically similar in their building blocks — they aren't. It's that the same abstract reaction category, condensation polymerization, underlies both processes: monomers join by forming a new bond while releasing a water molecule, whether the monomers are nucleotides (phosphodiester bonds, transcription) or amino acids (peptide bonds, translation). This is a mechanism-level bridge between Module 2's chemistry and Module 1's central-dogma property, not a claim that the molecules themselves are alike.
links: Central dogma at the molecular level · Condensation reactions link nucleic acids and proteins

title: Everyday phenomena, molecular explanations
prompt: Match each everyday phenomenon to the molecular-level concept it actually demonstrates.

pairs.left: Egg white turning solid and opaque when cooked
pairs.right: Heat disrupts the weak bonds (H-bonds, ionic interactions) holding tertiary structure — not the peptide bonds of the primary sequence

pairs.left: Dish soap lifting grease off a pan
pairs.right: Amphipathic molecules surround hydrophobic grease with their tails, forming micelles with hydrophilic heads facing the water

pairs.left: DNA strands separating when heated during PCR
pairs.right: Breaking hydrogen bonds between complementary bases — the phosphodiester backbone within each strand stays intact

pairs.left: Meat becoming tender when treated with a protease-based tenderizer
pairs.right: Enzymatic hydrolysis breaking peptide bonds, cutting long polypeptides into shorter fragments
Raising the stomach's pH by neutralizing excess H+, moving it back toward a range that denatures the stomach's own proteins less aggressively

explanation: All five are real-world instances of the same handful of Module 2 mechanisms — weak vs. strong bonds, amphipathic self-assembly, hydrolysis, and pH — showing up far outside a biology classroom.
links: Protein denaturation · Amphipathic molecules · Hydrogen bonds · Hydrolysis · pH

title: What actually happens when you cook an egg white
stem: Raw egg white is a clear, runny solution of the protein albumin, each molecule correctly folded into its normal tertiary structure. When heated, it turns white, opaque, and solid — and stays that way even after cooling back down. Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) The change is irreversible: cooling the cooked egg white does not return it to its original clear, runny state.

(나) The protein's amino acid sequence (primary structure) is identical before and after cooking.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Heat energy disrupted the weak interactions (hydrogen bonds, ionic interactions, hydrophobic clustering) holding the folded tertiary structure together, causing the protein to unfold and re-tangle into a disordered aggregate — this is denaturation.
statements.explanation: Denaturation is the loss of higher-order structure (secondary/tertiary/quaternary) without necessarily breaking the primary covalent backbone.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Because statement (나) says the primary structure is unchanged, the peptide bonds linking amino acids together were not broken by the heat.
statements.explanation: Peptide bonds are strong covalent bonds; ordinary cooking temperatures disrupt only the much weaker non-covalent interactions that maintain higher-order folding, leaving the covalent primary sequence intact.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Since the amino acid sequence is unchanged, the cooked protein could spontaneously refold back into its original functional shape if given enough time.
statements.explanation: Denaturation by heat typically causes irreversible aggregation — unfolded hydrophobic regions from many different protein molecules clump together randomly into a tangled solid mass that generally cannot spontaneously find its way back to the single correct folded structure.

links: Protein denaturation · Weak bonds vs. peptide bonds · Real-world: cooking

stem: PCR (a lab technique for copying DNA) begins by heating a DNA sample to ~95°C, which causes the double helix to separate into two single strands. The reaction then cools, and new strands are synthesized using each original strand as a template. What does the initial heating step break, and what does it leave intact?
options: It breaks the phosphodiester bonds within each strand, cutting the DNA into short fragments
It breaks the hydrogen bonds holding the two complementary strands together, while the phosphodiester bonds within each individual strand remain intact
It breaks the glycosidic bonds between each base and its sugar, releasing free bases
It has no chemical effect; the strands separate purely from physical agitation
It converts the DNA's deoxyribose sugars into ribose, temporarily turning it into RNA
explanation: The two strands of a DNA double helix are held together only by hydrogen bonds between complementary base pairs — comparatively weak interactions that heat energy can break. Each individual strand's own backbone (sugars linked by phosphodiester bonds) is held together by strong covalent bonds that ordinary heating does not touch, which is exactly why each separated strand survives intact and can serve as a template afterward.
links: Hydrogen bonds vs. phosphodiester bonds · Real-world: PCR

box: Penicillin works by blocking the enzyme that cross-links peptidoglycan strands, preventing bacteria from building a functional cell wall.
claim: Penicillin can selectively kill bacterial cells without directly damaging human cells because human cells have a plasma membrane but lack the peptidoglycan cell wall that penicillin's target enzyme acts on.
explanation: Bacterial (prokaryotic) cells rely on a rigid peptidoglycan cell wall for structural support and protection against osmotic pressure. Human cells are eukaryotic animal cells, which never have a cell wall at all — only a plasma membrane — so a drug that specifically disrupts cell-wall construction has no equivalent target in human cells, making it selectively toxic to bacteria.
links: Bacterial cell wall · Animal cells lack a wall · Real-world: selective antibiotics

box: Fish that live in near-freezing water tend to have a higher proportion of unsaturated fatty acids in their membrane phospholipids compared to mammals or warm-water species.
claim: This is an adaptive advantage because the kinks introduced by double bonds in unsaturated tails prevent the phospholipids from packing tightly together, which keeps the membrane fluid rather than freezing solid at low temperatures.
explanation: Saturated fatty acid tails are straight and pack tightly, tending to make membranes more rigid, especially as temperature drops. Unsaturated tails' kinks (from C=C double bonds) prevent that tight packing, keeping the membrane fluid enough to function even in cold water — the same structural principle tested elsewhere in this deck, now applied to a real evolutionary trade-off.
links: Saturated vs. unsaturated fatty acids · Membrane fluidity · Real-world: cold-adapted organisms

title: Why undigested lactose causes discomfort
stem: Lactose is a disaccharide (glucose + galactose) that must be broken down by the enzyme lactase before it can be absorbed in the small intestine. People with lactose intolerance produce too little lactase, so much of the lactose they consume reaches the large intestine undigested, where gut bacteria ferment it, producing gas and drawing in water. Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Lactase catalyzes the breakdown of lactose into its two monosaccharides.

(나) This breakdown reaction requires water as a reactant, not a product.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: The reaction lactase catalyzes is hydrolysis, since a bond is broken by consuming a water molecule rather than releasing one.
statements.explanation: Splitting a disaccharide into two monosaccharides by consuming a water molecule to break the glycosidic bond is the definition of hydrolysis — the reverse of the condensation reaction that built the bond in the first place.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Lactase speeds up this reaction as a catalyst, but doesn't change whether the reaction is energetically favorable — hydrolysis of lactose would still release energy even without the enzyme present, just far too slowly to matter physiologically.
statements.explanation: Enzymes lower activation energy to increase reaction rate; they don't change the underlying energetics (favorability) of a reaction.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Since lactose intolerance means lactase is completely absent, no lactose at all can ever be broken down in these individuals.
statements.explanation: Lactose intolerance is typically a matter of reduced lactase levels or activity, not necessarily complete absence — most lactose-intolerant individuals can still digest small amounts, which is why symptoms are often dose-dependent.

links: Hydrolysis · Enzymes as catalysts · Real-world: lactose intolerance

stem: Dish soap molecules have a long nonpolar hydrocarbon tail and a charged, polar head. When soap is added to a greasy pan full of water, the soap molecules arrange themselves into spherical clusters called micelles, with grease trapped in the center. Which arrangement of the soap molecules within a micelle correctly explains why this works?
options: Polar heads cluster in the center, facing away from both the water and the grease
Nonpolar tails face outward into the water, since like dissolves like
Nonpolar tails point inward, dissolving into the trapped grease, while polar heads face outward into the surrounding water
The soap molecules form a rigid crystal lattice around the grease, similar to how NaCl forms a solid
Soap chemically reacts with the grease, converting it into a water-soluble molecule
explanation: This is the same amphipathic self-assembly principle behind a phospholipid bilayer, applied to a single-layer sphere instead of a two-layer sheet: soap's hydrophobic tails avoid water by clustering around and dissolving into the grease at the center, while its hydrophilic heads stay in contact with the surrounding water on the micelle's outer surface. That arrangement is what lets the whole grease-filled micelle rinse away in water, even though grease alone is insoluble in water.
links: Amphipathic molecules · Micelle formation · Real-world: soap and grease

box: Intravenous (IV) saline solution is prepared by dissolving solid NaCl in sterile water until it reaches a specific concentration before being administered into a patient's bloodstream.
claim: This dissolving process works because water's partially negative oxygen atoms surround and stabilize each Na+ ion, while water's partially positive hydrogen atoms surround and stabilize each Cl– ion, pulling the ionic lattice apart into individual hydrated ions.
explanation: This is water acting as the "universal solvent" for ionic compounds: water's polarity lets it form hydration shells around each separated ion — oxygen (δ–) facing cations like Na+, hydrogen (δ+) facing anions like Cl– — which stabilizes the separated ions in solution and is exactly why an ionic solid like NaCl dissolves in water, whether in a beaker or in an IV bag.
links: Hydration shells · Water as universal solvent · Real-world: IV saline
